newsitem.title: ANGOLA: UNITA deputies arrive in Angolan capital.
newsitem.headline: UNITA deputies arrive in Angolan capital.

text.p: Senior members of the former rebel UNITA movement arrived in the Angolan capital on Monday, but it was not clear if a government of national unity would be formed as scheduled later this week.
Officials said around 50 UNITA deputies had arrived, fewer than the 70 expected in the capital on U.N. flights from Bailundo, in Angola's central highlands.
U.N. special representative Alioune Blondin Beye, who was at the airport to welcome the deputies, said he would meet UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi on Tuesday, apparently to clarify the situation.
"I am going down to Bailundo tomorrow for talks with Savimbi," he told reporters without elaborating.

UNITA spokesman Isaias Samakuva said he hoped the rest of the deputies would arrive on Tuesday, and thought it would be useful for UNITA and the ruling MPLA to discuss the programme of a new government.

There was no sign that the UNITA deputies would be sworn in during the next few days and it was also not clear if plans for the inauguration of the unity government would go ahead as planned on March 20.
Diplomats at the airport to meet the UNITA members declined to comment.
The arrival of the UNITA officials is a key step for the establishment of a unity government which will include members of UNITA and the ruling MPLA.

The inauguration was originally planned for January 25 but postponed several times, mainly because of problems in finding an acceptable role for UNITA leader Savimbi, who controls much of Angola, including diamond-rich areas.
UNITA and the government signed a peace accord in 1994 which has brought Angola its longest period of relative peace since two decades of civil war erupted on independence from Portugal in 1975.

The U.N. has around 7,000 troops, military observers and civilian police from more than 30 countries in Angola, helping to implement the accord, which provides for demobilisation of thousands of former rebels and government fighters and the formation of a united army.

The mandate of the U.N. peacekeeping mission, UNAVEM, ends on March 31, and the Security Council has been keeping a close eye on the process, blaming UNITA for delays and threatening action against the former rebels.
Even after UNAVEM ends its mandate and completes its withdrawal over several months, it is expected to be succeeded by a smaller U.N. observer mission that would remain until the end of the year.
